quote: I have to think about this. My my son and daughter-in-law had, I guess, it was Duke Power.
stewart_read: This is a soft stall dressed as a comparison anecdote (free program elsewhere) rather than a hard objection, but it's still an opening to reframe: the free-program story is actually a chance to contrast with Ion's guaranteed-savings bill swap. Rep instead answers narrowly ('Oh, I don't think so') and lets her keep control of the thread toward 'let me talk to my neighbor.'
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep simply didn't have information about competitor/utility programs and answered honestly, which is defensible knowledge-gap handling, not a missed flip.
coaching_implication: When a customer brings up a free/alternative program as a reason to delay, redirect back to the specific guarantee just pitched ('the bill swap') rather than answering the tangent literally — keeps the conversation anchored on Ion's offer instead of drifting to a third-party story.

quote: Well because I just billed out estimates and quotes. So if you want, I can help you build one real quick, and then you can just get an offer. You don't even have to make any decisions.
stewart_read: Rep substitutes a low-commitment ask (build a quote, no decision required) for the harder ask (book now), successfully converting her 'let me ask my neighbor' stall into forward motion.
coaching_implication: This is a repeatable move worth reinforcing with the rep — good use of a no-commitment reframe to keep a stalling customer moving through verify.

quote: Well, you can see that it has a good many trees in the area that's between us and the sun in the west.
stewart_read: Customer gives specific, escalating detail about shading (leaves not out yet, tall trees, tall house, neighbor's own shading problem) — a real technical concern, not a stall. Rep's response stays surface-level ('It doesn't look too bad, though') without acknowledging the leaves-not-out timing detail she's flagging as a reason his satellite read may be misleading.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: rep correctly punts the technical assessment to 'the specialist' rather than getting pulled into scope creep debating satellite imagery accuracy — this is schema-correct per setter_scope_discipline.
coaching_implication: The scope-hold is correct; the miss is not naming her specific point (that the satellite image is a snapshot without leaves) before pivoting to the specialist. A one-line acknowledgment would land as heard rather than brushed off.

quote: I had a, like, a $350 bill. It's usually from $1.50 to $2.50, I think.
stewart_read: A strong anchor point — a recent bill spike plus a stated normal range — captured cleanly by the rep ('Okay. So $1.50 to $2.50... Let me put that down'), but never flipped into the bill-swap savings framing already pitched at 01:05.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to circle back to this number when booking or closing the call — e.g., tie the appointment directly to 'seeing what the bill swap looks like against that $150-250 range' to reinforce the reason for the appointment.

quote: Let me ask you this. How long have you guys been in business?
stewart_read: An unprompted, late-call legitimacy question is a positive engagement signal — she is actively vetting the company because she is now considering moving forward, not stalling.
coaching_implication: Manager should note this as evidence the rep's patient handling of earlier friction (bill photo navigation) paid off in trust; worth pointing out to the rep as a signal their approach worked.

quote: The only thing they ask is that you're not driving and you're able to access your email.
stewart_read: Schema's button-up language specifies the customer should be able to 'sit down to review the design on your computer,' not 'access your email.' This is a substantive drift — it sets the wrong expectation for what the appointment will require (email access vs. active screen-share/design review), which can affect show-up readiness.
coaching_implication: Correct the rep's button-up phrasing to the schema's computer/screen framing so the customer arrives prepared to review a live design, not just check email.

quote: Do you all do also do, like, if you had a field, stick them in a field?
stewart_read: Customer asks about ground-mount panels, a legitimate product question outside standard rooftop scope. Rep transparently admits he doesn't know and defers cleanly: 'Oh, I I don't know any of that. Dispatch kits will, though. So you can ask tomorrow.'
coaching_implication: This is the correct knowledge-gap pattern — admit and redirect to the specialist rather than guess or fabricate. Reinforce this as good practice; also flag for the closer's handoff so the question isn't dropped.

quote: Okay. Alright. Thanks, hon. Alright. Thank you. You have a great day.
stewart_read: The call closes warmly but without a full button-up handshake — no explicit 'is that fair?' confirmation, no stated one-hour block, and the driving/computer line was already drifted from script. The date/time was reconfirmed once ('the twenty fourth, tomorrow, Tuesday at 12:00') but the close lacks the full procedural close-out the schema specifies.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: given the warm rapport already built by this point (she's asking her own trust questions), a lighter close may be low-risk — but the schema treats these elements as required regardless of rapport level.
coaching_implication: Build the full button-up checklist into muscle memory: one-hour block statement, 'is that fair?' handshake, and correct no-driving/computer framing, even when the customer sounds sold — this is what protects show rate.
